title: Arrival at Outpost Echo

beats.narrativeText: After the long journey, the learner finally arrives at Outpost Echo — and the station is silent. Not the silence of a place that was never used, but the silence of a place that stopped mid-sentence.

Everything looks quiet, but nothing looks abandoned the way it should. Equipment sits exactly where it was left. Doors are unlocked. Observation boards still show notes nobody ever finished writing. Whoever was here didn't plan to be gone this long.
Atlas guides the learner through an initial survey of the station, walking the map together and working out what each area was actually used for.
As the survey continues, the learner starts noticing small things that don't quite add up — the first hints that something happened here that nobody planned for.
The learner must turn their own survey into a simple sketch map of the station — not a copy of anyone else's, but one built entirely from what they've actually seen.
With the sketch map finished, Outpost Echo finally has a shape the learner can hold in their head — the first real sense of where they are, and what still needs investigating.
The learner reflects on the untouched equipment and the unfinished notes — and on the question neither of those things has answered yet: why did everyone leave without finishing?
The survey is complete, but the questions it raised aren't. Something happened at Outpost Echo — and the first real hints of what are only just starting to surface.

activities.title: Explore Station Map
activities.storyContext: Atlas pulls up a basic map of Outpost Echo — the first real look at the place the learner will be investigating for weeks to come.
activities.instructions: Walk through the station map with Atlas. Note the main areas you pass and how they connect to each other — you'll need this later, so pay attention now rather than trying to remember it afterwards.
activities.output: A list of the station's main areas in the Explorer Journal.

activities.title: Label Important Areas
activities.storyContext: A map with no labels is just a shape — knowing what each area actually was will matter the moment an investigation sends you back to one of them.
activities.instructions: Label the important areas of the station map, such as the laboratory, observatory and living quarters.

activities.title: Record Unusual Observations
activities.storyContext: Equipment sits exactly where it was left, and the observation boards still show notes nobody finished writing — as if the whole station paused mid-task.
activities.instructions: As you explore, record anything unusual you notice in your Explorer Journal — especially anything that looks interrupted rather than simply old.

activities.title: Produce a Simple Sketch Map
activities.storyContext: A clear map will help the learner navigate Outpost Echo in every mission still to come.
activities.instructions: Draw a simple sketch map of the station based on your own survey — what you actually saw and labelled, not what you think a map of a research station should look like.
activities.output: A hand-drawn sketch map of Outpost Echo.

activities.title: Improve the Station Map
activities.storyContext: A well-made map uses symbols so anyone can read it quickly.
activities.instructions: Add symbols and a key to your sketch map to make it easier to read.
activities.output: An improved sketch map with a symbol key.

activities.title: How Are Research Stations Organised?
activities.storyContext: Outpost Echo was built to follow the same principles as real research stations.
activities.instructions: Find out how a real scientific research station is organised and compare it with Outpost Echo.
activities.output: None required — this is an open investigation.

prompts: Which detail made you feel like something at Outpost Echo was left unfinished, and why did it stand out to you?

discussionPoints: What did the station's layout tell you about how the expedition worked?
What would you want to explore first if you arrived somewhere new?
parentGuide.preparation: No special preparation required. A ruler is useful for the sketch map.
parentGuide.assessment: Look for a clearly labelled sketch map and specific, descriptive observations rather than vague statements.

completionCriteria: Station map explored, important areas labelled, and a sketch map produced.
